precepts.text: Manasseh's coast reached to the sea and included the inhabitants of Dor and her towns.
precepts.point: He lived at Caesarea Maritima, the old Strato's Tower below Dor, in the land of West Manasseh. He was devout, gave alms to the people and prayed always, like Tobit.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.why:
Where is Cornelius from? Some people say Italy. He is from Cesarea. There are three Caesareas: one in Africa, which is not written of, Caesarea Philippi, and Caesarea Maritima. Cornelius is from Caesarea Maritima, the place the maps call Strato's Tower, right under Dor, in Samaria, the same country where Christ spoke to the woman at the well. When Rome colonized our land they named it for Caesar, and Maritima because it is a port on the water. And the maps mark that land West Manasseh.

Somebody will say that's just a map, it ain't in the Bible. So here it is in the Bible, for the doubters: “And the coast of Manasseh was from Asher to Michmethah, that lieth before Shechem; and the border went along on the right hand unto the inhabitants of En–tappuah.”

Read on. “Now Manasseh had the land of Tappuah: but Tappuah on the border of Manasseh belonged to the children of Ephraim”. The coast went down to the river Kanah: “the coast of Manasseh also was on the north side of the river, and the outgoings of it were at the sea”. “Southward it was Ephraim’s, and northward it was Manasseh’s, and the sea is his border”: the Mediterranean Sea. Peter dwelt in Joppa and went some thirty to forty miles up the coast to Caesarea Maritima, just before Dor.

Then verse 11: “And Manasseh had in Issachar and in Asher Beth–shean and her towns, and Ibleam and her towns, and the inhabitants of Dor and her towns”. Under Dor was Caesarea Maritima; that was all Dor before. Endor, Taanach and Megiddo were Manasseh's too. “Yet the children of Manasseh could not drive out the inhabitants of those cities; but the Canaanites would dwell in that land.” There were too many of them to conquer them all.

So that is Manasseh's land. It is called West Manasseh because Manasseh also dwelt on the other side of Jordan, East Manasseh. This was once Manasseh's allotment right under Ephraim, the sons of Joseph. Asher shared that port, but the land was Manasseh's.

Cornelius was not Italian. He was of the Italian band, a unit of the Roman army. There were Israelites in Rome's military, just as there are Israelites in America's military today. But negroes love master so much they see the word Italian and get excited: yes, he's white, I knew it. No, he was of the Italian band, from Caesarea, West Manasseh, one of the northern kingdom. A centurion was over a hundred men. He was “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway”, the exact same thing Tobit said he did.

precepts.text: Joseph is a fruitful bough; the fruitfulness of Joseph's seed was prophesied by Israel.
precepts.point: Their fruitfulness was prophesied when Israel blessed Joseph; the very name Ephraim goes into being fruitful.

note.label: Joshua 17: The Lot of Manasseh and the Blessing of Ephraim

precepts.why:
The children of Joseph complain, “Why hast thou given me but one lot and one portion to inherit, seeing I am a great people”. Great means numerous: Ephraim and Manasseh were among the most populated tribes, and Ephraim's own portion had already been given back in chapter 16.

That fruitfulness was prophesied when Israel blessed Joseph: “Joseph is a fruitful bough, even a fruitful bough by a well; whose branches run over the wall”. The very name Ephraim goes into being fruitful. So a great people is exactly what Israel said Joseph's seed would be.

Joshua answered without bias: “If thou be a great people, then get thee up to the wood country”, into the forest, and cut down there in the land of the Perizzites and of the giants, “if mount Ephraim be too narrow for thee.” Narrow means too small: if you are complaining that your lot is too small, then go to war and conquer more land.

precepts.text: Joseph brought his two sons Manasseh and Ephraim to his sick father, and Israel strengthened himself and sat upon the bed, glad to see his son.
precepts.point: Manasseh had issues driving the Canaanites out, but Ephraim did it. The difference between the two brothers goes back to Genesis 48, where Israel blessed Joseph's sons and crossed his hands, guiding them wittingly, meaning he knew exactly what he was doing.

note.label: Joshua 17: The Lot of Manasseh and the Blessing of Ephraim

precepts.why:
Joshua tells the house of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, “Thou art a great people, and hast great power”, and that they shall drive out the Canaanites though they have iron chariots. Manasseh had issues driving the Canaanites out, but Ephraim did it. The difference between the two brothers goes back to Genesis 48.

“And it came to pass after these things, that one told Joseph, Behold, thy father is sick: and he took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.” Joseph brought his two sons to his sick father, “and Israel strengthened himself, and sat upon the bed”, glad to see his son. This is the moment the two brothers were blessed, and where Ephraim's greater place began.

precepts.text: Israel's eyes were dim for age; he kissed and embraced Joseph's sons, saying he had not thought to see Joseph's face, and lo, God had shewed him his seed also.
precepts.point: Manasseh had issues driving the Canaanites out, but Ephraim did it. The difference between the two brothers goes back to Genesis 48, where Israel blessed Joseph's sons and crossed his hands, guiding them wittingly, meaning he knew exactly what he was doing.

note.label: Joshua 17: The Lot of Manasseh and the Blessing of Ephraim

precepts.why:
“And Israel beheld Joseph’s sons, and said, Who are these? And Joseph said unto his father, They are my sons, whom God hath given me in this place.” Israel says bring them to me and I will bless them. “Now the eyes of Israel were dim for age, so that he could not see.” He kissed them and embraced them, and said, “I had not thought to see thy face: and, lo, God hath shewed me also thy seed.”

Israel's eyes were dim for age; he could not see which son was which. Remember that, because what he does with his hands next is not by sight.

precepts.text: Joseph set Manasseh toward Israel's right hand for the greater blessing of the firstborn, but Israel stretched his right hand upon Ephraim the younger, guiding his hands wittingly.
precepts.point: Manasseh had issues driving the Canaanites out, but Ephraim did it. The difference between the two brothers goes back to Genesis 48, where Israel blessed Joseph's sons and crossed his hands, guiding them wittingly, meaning he knew exactly what he was doing.

note.label: Joshua 17: The Lot of Manasseh and the Blessing of Ephraim

precepts.why:
“And Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel’s right hand, and brought them near unto him.” Joseph set Manasseh toward Israel's right hand for the greater blessing of the firstborn. “And Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it upon Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand upon Manasseh’s head, guiding his hands wittingly; for Manasseh was the firstborn.”

Israel crossed his hands, guiding them wittingly, meaning he knew exactly what he was doing. His eyes were dim, but this was no mistake. The right hand went on Ephraim the younger, and that is the root of why Ephraim drove out the Canaanites where Manasseh had issues.

precepts.text: It displeased Joseph and he held up his father's hand, but Israel refused, saying I know it, my son: Manasseh shall also be great, but his younger brother shall be greater, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations.
precepts.point: Manasseh had issues driving the Canaanites out, but Ephraim did it. The difference between the two brothers goes back to Genesis 48, where Israel blessed Joseph's sons and crossed his hands, guiding them wittingly, meaning he knew exactly what he was doing.

note.label: Joshua 17: The Lot of Manasseh and the Blessing of Ephraim

precepts.why:
“And when Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand upon the head of Ephraim, it displeased him: and he held up his father’s hand, to remove it from Ephraim’s head unto Manasseh’s head.” Joseph said, “Not so, my father: for this is the firstborn”. “And his father refused, and said, I know it, my son, I know it: he also shall become a people, and he also shall be great: but truly his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations.”

Manasseh shall also be great, but Ephraim shall be greater. That is why Joshua can say to the house of Joseph, “thou shalt drive out the Canaanites, though they have iron chariots, and though they be strong”, and it is Ephraim that did it. Ephraim being greater goes into Ephraim becoming the head of the ten tribes, the head of the kingdom of Samaria; and it was Ephraim that led the charge, with the help of Issachar and Manasseh, that brought the ten tribes from the eastern hemisphere to the western hemisphere.

The Zondervan compact Bible dictionary, a tool to add to your arsenal, says Ephraim and Manasseh seem to have been bitter rivals, Manasseh being the larger group, but Ephraim asserting the more vigorous leadership, though they seem to have held their land in common for a time. Vigorous means very passionate, sometimes rough; that is the spirit the children of Ephraim have.

precepts.text: Joseph's horns are the horns of unicorns, and with them he shall push the people together to the ends of the earth; they are the ten thousands of Ephraim and the thousands of Manasseh.

precepts.why:
Joshua says the house of Joseph “hast great power”. Moses said the same of Joseph: “His glory is like the firstling of his bullock, and his horns are like the horns of unicorns: with them he shall push the people together to the ends of the earth: and they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh.”

The unicorn there is not a fairy tale horse; the original etymology goes into the rhinoceros. With those horns Joseph pushes the people together to the ends of the earth, and notice the order: the ten thousands of Ephraim and the thousands of Manasseh. It was Ephraim that led the charge, with the help of Issachar and Manasseh, that brought the ten tribes from the eastern hemisphere to the western hemisphere.

The greatness Joshua speaks of, “Thou art a great people, and hast great power”, grew into Ephraim standing at the head of the northern kingdom.

note.label: Joshua 17: The Lot of Manasseh and the Blessing of Ephraim

precepts.why:
In Judges 7 Manasseh went to war with the three hundred men and destroyed the Midianites though they were lower in numbers, because Christ gave them the victory. Then in Judges 8: “And the men of Ephraim said unto him, Why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not, when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? And they did chide with him sharply.”

Ephraim was upset that they were not called to help in that war. That war-like spirit was always in Ephraim; they always had that leadership attribute, that military spirit, the vigorous leadership. It is the same spirit that drove out the Canaanites with their iron chariots, where Manasseh had issues.

points: A lot goes into an allotment, a portion; there was a portion for the tribe of Manasseh, for he was the firstborn of Joseph. Machir, the firstborn of Manasseh and the father of Gilead, was a man of war, therefore he had Gilead and Bashan.

Bashan was the kingdom of Og, one of the giants that Israel conquered under Joshua. Before the conquest all this territory was called the land of Canaan, with the Canaanites, the Perizzites, and the Jebusites and their families dwelling in it.

Prior to this chapter Judah received his inheritance in chapter 15 and the inheritance of Joseph, Ephraim, came in chapter 16; after the victories the Most High gave through Christ, the land was divided by lot so that every tribe had its portion.

The Bible maps that even the enemies of Israel put together according to the scriptures show this history: Manasseh held Bashan and a portion by Gilead on the other side of Jordan. The so-called Cubans come from this tribe; this is their history that their enemies do not want them to know.
